aldemar.headline: Walmart confirms what the retail-sales print hinted — and BAC closes through its line
aldemar.standfirst: Thursday the consumer story stopped being a data point and became a company: Walmart fell 8.8% on results and an outlook that missed, the S&P dropped 0.86% to 7,641 and the VIX jumped 7.7% to 16 — its highest close in a month — while Brent surged 2.4% to $93.78 as three China-linked supertankers turned back from the strait. In the book, BAC closed at 61.86, through the 62 support your thesis named, with both stops now within one bad session. Today is monthly OPEX: the dealer pin that has damped every move for two weeks comes off tonight.

positions.title: 1 signal on BAC — read before the open (INTC quiet)

items.html: BAC — BAC −2.07% to 61.86 — through the 62 support, on the day Walmart repriced the US consumer. This is the risk the thesis carried from day one arriving on schedule: the biggest retailer in the country cut its outlook, and a bank with a large card book trades as a levered bet on that same consumer. The steepener half of the story is intact — the 10-year rose back to 4.70% — but credit fear beat margin math on Thursday, and the close under 62 removes the support your entry leaned on. Gabriel is −3.91% on entry at −0.63R with the stop at 60.39, 2.4% below; Aldemar −3.58% at −0.51R, stop 59.65, 3.7% below. The plan already answers this: the stop is the exit, and it is close enough now that no averaging, widening, or hoping belongs anywhere near this position. A reclaim of 62 on Monday's post-OPEX tape would be the first sign the break was expiry noise rather than trend.

INTC — INTC −0.72% to 92.13 after touching 89.85 — held under the offer price but stopped falling. An intraday dip through 90 that closed back above it, on no new company news, while the sector digested Walmart's macro message. Aldemar is −12.9% on entry at −0.55R — a touch past half the risk unit — with the 81.10 stop 13.6% below. Nothing to do; the wide stop was bought precisely so days like this are noise rather than decisions.

positions.note: Signal changes the thesis, the levels or the size — earnings, a regulator with teeth, M&A, a ruling with a revenue line attached. Everything else is filed as noise on purpose; a real signal survives skepticism.

themes.right: supertankers turning back · Brent $93.78 · Gulf states picking sides
themes.title: The strait empties from both ends — now China's tankers are turning around

items.html: Three China-linked supertankers turn back from the strait; another vessel reportedly struck by a projectile. Chinese-linked tonnage was the last large buyer-side flow still testing the blockade — when those turn around, the strait's effective closure is no longer a Western sanctions story but a physical one for everyone. Each incident adds to a war-risk premium that no longer washes out between headlines.

Brent +2.4% to $93.78, the highest since the ceasefire; WTI closes 86.62. A fifth advance in six sessions, and now with acceleration. At these levels the pass-through into September CPI is no longer a scenario — it is arithmetic, and it is the single strongest force holding the Policy-tightening regime alive.

UAE moves to sanctions against Iran as Gulf states pick sides. Tuesday's missiles into UAE waters are producing exactly the alignment Tehran could least afford: the neighbourhood joining the economic squeeze. It widens the war's financial front and shrinks Iran's remaining trade routes.

themes.note: The transmission is oil → inflation → the regime call, and it is compounding: crude at $93.78 with yields back at 4.70% is the bond market repricing the same war twice — once as supply shock, once as deficit. Gold holding its record bid through a second day says the hedgers are not treating Wednesday as a spike. For the book, the war now cuts against both BAC positions through the consumer-and-credit channel while the OPEX reset tonight removes the dealer dampening that kept all of this orderly. Monday's open is the first honest tape in two weeks — respect what it shows.

world.title: The consumer bid breaks: Walmart −8.8%, the VIX wakes up, and the pin comes off tonight

items.html: Walmart falls 8.8% on a miss and soft outlook — the week's retail test failed at the biggest desk. Home Depot's beat on Tuesday said the consumer was fine; Walmart's guidance says the opposite, and Walmart sees more of the consumer than anyone. After a −0.6% retail-sales print and sentiment at 51, the weight of evidence has shifted — this is now a consumer-slowdown tape until proven otherwise.

Wednesday's Treasury relief fades — the 10-year back to 4.70%, the 30-year 5.25%; Bessent floats expanding buybacks beyond $4B per issue. One day after the buyback headline, the long end took the yields right back. When official buying only holds the line for a session, the market is telling you the supply-and-inflation pressure underneath is bigger than the intervention.

S&P −0.86% to 7,641, Nasdaq −1.0%, VIX +7.7% to 16.04 — the highest volatility close in a month, with monthly OPEX today. Four red days in five, and the first one where volatility confirmed the move. Tonight the monthly expiry rolls off roughly $80B of dealer gamma and the walls and flip reset Monday — ranges typically widen after, and this time they widen into a consumer scare and a $93 Brent.

Gold holds the record zone with a second green day. No give-back after Wednesday's historic move — consolidation at the highs on a risk-off day is the strong-hands pattern. The debasement-and-war trade is now a position, not an event.

aldemar.ondeck: Monthly OPEX today — Monthly expiry. Dealer gamma rolls off and the levels reset on Monday.

weekly.headline: The week the market started auditing the AI bill — and the war stopped pretending
weekly.standfirst: Five sessions, a third straight weekly gain, and a record close on Thursday: the S&P added 0.36% to 7,785.76 while the VIX fell to 14.25. Underneath that calm, two things changed. Investors began pricing how AI infrastructure is financed rather than what it might earn — Alphabet on Tuesday, Broadcom and Applied Materials on Friday — while the CPU side of the same trade got re-rated upward. And the war moved from rhetoric to enforcement: a US helicopter disabled a tanker running the blockade, Hormuz traffic sank to three-month lows, and the interim deal now expires on Tuesday.

Two inflation prints cooled, one consumer cracked, and the AI trade split in half

TECHThe AI capex audit begins: GOOG −3.6% Tuesday on a $25bn bond deal, AVGO −6% Friday on a $370bn financing question. Alphabet's quarterly capex hit $44.9bn with free cash flow negative for the first time; Broadcom was marked down on how a lease-and-debt structure gets funded. The market spent this week deciding that the cost of the build belongs in the valuation.TradingKey · Yahoo Finance · 11–14 Aug
SEMISBofA lifts the 2030 CPU market from $170bn to $210bn — INTC ran 6.3% Thursday before fading 2.0% Friday. Vivek Arya's argument is that AI moving from training to inference resets the GPU-to-CPU ratio toward 1:1. It is the bull case for both INTC positions, and Friday showed it will not travel in a straight line.Motley Fool · BofA · 13 Aug
DATACPI cooled Wednesday, PPI cooled Thursday to 4.7% from 5.5%, then retail sales fell 0.6% Friday. Three prints that moved September from a coin flip to a hold. The tone changed midweek: the first two were disinflation, the third was demand weakening — the same direction with a very different meaning for earnings.BLS · AP · 12–14 Aug
RATESThe 30-year auction clears at 5.216% — the highest in a quarter century. The long end refused to follow the cooler prints down, which is a fiscal and energy verdict rather than a policy one. It is the single cleanest reason to be long a bank here.Yahoo Finance · 14 Aug
NOISEFiled and ignored: Pixel 11 previews, an Alphabet 11-year retrospective, a $107.66 Intel target already overtaken. A week's worth of commentary that arrived after the moves it described. None of it touched a thesis, a level or a size.various · 10–14 Aug

The through-line is that this market has stopped paying for AI ambition and started pricing AI arithmetic — who is writing the cheques versus who is cashing them. You now hold one of each: Alphabet writing them, Intel cashing them.

From rhetoric to Hellfire missiles in five sessions

STRIKEA US Navy helicopter disables the M/V Vela Nova with two Hellfire missiles in the Gulf of Oman. The first commercial vessel fired on since the ceasefire, and the moment the blockade stopped being a declaration. Engine room and steering gear, deliberately disabling rather than sinking.12 Aug
SHIPPINGHormuz traffic falls to near three-month lows as both sides claim control. Trump says the strait is open under US control; Iran says nothing passes without its permission. The traffic data settles it — whoever is right, the tankers are not sailing.13 Aug
MILITARYHegseth: the blockade can hold "indefinitely"; a relief carrier group sails Friday. Words backed by a rotation schedule. The market's hope that enforcement fades on its own was removed this week.13–14 Aug
OILWTI rose 4.7% on the week to 81.84 while equities made a record. Energy finished as the week's best sector. Crude is carrying the war risk that the equity indices are not.10–14 Aug

The week's arc runs from talks-are-close on Monday to a missile strike on Tuesday to annexation talk on Friday. Nothing was signed, and the June interim deal now expires on Tuesday 18 August with the blockade live and both sides demanding compensation from the other.
